_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: Gemara. Granted that a mere prohibition taking effect on a prohibition he does not hold: for example, one who eats the carcass of a non-kosher animal is not liable on account of a carcass [nevela], since that is a mere prohibition, neither inclusive nor expanded.
rashi:a2.1: Since he became prohibited in [pure] pieces [the word “pure” is printed in parentheses]: he became prohibited also with regard to the fat, because of impurity. This is an inclusive prohibition: the prohibition was not added to the object but to the man. Since a prohibition was added for him with regard to other things, it includes this too in the prohibition.
rashi:a3.1: The prohibition of benefit: this is an expanded prohibition, since a prohibition was added to the object.
rashi:a4.1: Notar: this too is an expanded prohibition.
rashi:a4.2: Yom Kippur: an inclusive prohibition, since a prohibition was added to the man with regard to something that had been permitted to him until now.
rashi:a5.1: It does not speak of two animals, and notar and piggul are not found in one animal: since piggul arises only through the four rites of the blood. Therefore, once he rendered it piggul, it is fit neither for human eating nor for the altar’s eating, and so notar does not take effect on it.
rashi:a6.1: Its piggul status was abrogated: since the altar sanctified it through the rite. Ulla’s reason is explained in Zevaḥim (43a).
rashi:a9.1: If the majority is on the altar, throw it on the altar: the whole limb [counts as] on the altar, and all of it is notar, and so on.
rashi:a10.1: Does one follow the majority with regard to limbs, and so on: this dilemma is in the chapter Behema HaMaksha (Ḥullin 70a).
rashi:a10.2: One olive-bulk: it speaks of [one olive-bulk of] forbidden fat; it does not speak of two olive-bulks of fat.
rashi:a11.1: A date-bulk contains two olive-bulks: since that is what the throat holds.
rashi:a12.1: For example, where he ate a kidney with its fat: for eating the fat he is liable to three sin offerings and a guilt offering, and it also counts toward completing the eating of a date-bulk, while the olive-bulk of kidney completes the date-bulk. Therefore it does not teach piggul, since it does not speak of two olive-bulks of fat. And if you say: let it be established where he brought the olive-bulk of kidney up onto the altar, so that the fat is piggul and the kidney notar; if so, the notar does not apply to the olive-bulk of fat, and we need them all to apply to one [olive-bulk], since it teaches “eating,” that is, an olive-bulk.
rashi:a12.2: [A marginal gloss:] Rather, it speaks of one olive-bulk; and if he placed half the olive-bulk on the altar, there is no burning of less than an olive-bulk.
rashi:a12.3: For example, where he ate a kidney with its fat: and if you should wish to say, let him be liable for the kidney on account of piggul and for its fat on account of notar, one cannot say so, since it teaches “an impure person who ate” [forbidden fat]; it wants to establish all the prohibitions in the fat itself. This is my teacher’s explanation.
rashi:a12.4: Rav Pappa said: the reason it does not teach piggul is that it does not speak of two olive-bulks of fat. And as for what troubled you about the date-bulk: for example, where he filled out the fat with dates and completed it to a date-bulk.
rashi:a13.1: And he resolves it as where he ate an olive-bulk of piggul: from another animal, together with it.
rashi:a15.1: And let it teach: if he carried it out he is liable: since it is Yom Kippur.
rashi:a17.1: Appointed: one whom they designated the day before to lead away the goat.
rashi:a18.1: That is to say: since it teaches “even on Shabbat,” there is no joining and carrying for Yom Kippur. For if there were a prohibition of carrying on Yom Kippur, why was it necessary to include Shabbat? It overrides Yom Kippur, and the same would apply to Shabbat.
rashi:a19.1: Perhaps: from Yom Kippur we would not learn about Shabbat, since Yom Kippur is different, as the fulfillment of its mitzva is in this, like the daily offerings that are sacrificed on Shabbat.
rashi:a20.1: Mishna. His daughter and his sister: where he had intercourse with his mother and fathered her.
rashi:a20.2: And the wife of his brother: where she married him [his brother] beforehand, and after his death his father’s brother married her, and this man, her father, had intercourse with her while she was menstruating.
tosafot:a5.1: And notar and piggul are not found in one animal: this implies that if notar took effect on piggul, it would have had to teach five sin offerings. And this is puzzling: one could not find five, since one who eats sacrificial food while his body is impure is not liable for piggul, because it is not permitted to the pure and it never had a time of fitness. It should have said: notar, piggul and impurity are not found in one animal.
tosafot:a7.1: Ulla said: a handful of piggul, and so on: And if you ask: why does it not challenge from a limb itself? For it says in the chapter HaMizbe’aḥ Mekadesh (Zevaḥim 84a and 85b) that [an offering] one slaughtered [with intent to eat it] beyond its time, and so on: if they went up they do not come down; so too, if they came down they do not go up. And Ulla said: they taught this only where the fire has not taken hold of it, but where the fire has taken hold of it, even if they came down they go up. If so, we learn that it becomes the altar’s food and its piggul status is abrogated. One may say: in any case it is not taught there as explicitly that its piggul status is abrogated as it is explicitly taught with the handful.
tosafot:a7.2: Its piggul status is abrogated: In Menaḥot, in the chapter HaKometz (14a), Rashi asked why a verse is needed to exclude the handful from piggul; let me derive it from the fact that what permits it was not offered as commanded. He answered that it speaks where the fire took hold of most of it, so that the remainder was permitted, as we say: from when does the handful permit the remainder to be eaten? From when the fire has caught in most of it. But this is difficult: if so, its piggul status would be abrogated, as is evident here. One may say that it speaks where he brought half of it up onto the altar and half he did not, and its piggul status is not abrogated from the half that remained. And if you ask: even initially one brings it up, as we say in the chapter Beit Shammai (Zevaḥim 43b): a handful half of which he set on the ground, we bring it up even initially. One may say: there it is different, since all of it was on the altar at first and afterward he brought half of it down, but here it was not on the altar. And if you ask: the meal offering of libations and the meal offering of the anointed priest, which are burned whole, why is a verse needed to exclude them from piggul, when they permit nothing? One may say: since they were sanctified in the vessel, it is as if what permits them was offered, and it fixed them in piggul; therefore a verse is needed to exclude them.
tosafot:a10.1: Resolve the dilemma that Rami bar Ḥama raised: does one follow the majority with regard to limbs: The Kuntres [Rashi] explained that this is the dilemma in the chapter Behema HaMaksha (Ḥullin 70a). This does not seem right to Rabbeinu Tam, for what does that dilemma have to do with this one? There it concerns whether, if half came out with the majority of a limb, it counts as born or not. Therefore it seems one should explain that it is the dilemma in the chapter Mizbe’aḥ Mekadesh (Zevaḥim 87a), where they asked whether the airspace of the altar is like the altar or not, and so on: if most of it is over the ramp it is like the ramp; if most of it is over the altar it is like the altar. Resolve the dilemma of Rami bar Ḥama: whether there is joining with regard to burnt offerings or not.
tosafot:a12.1: For example, where he ate a kidney with its fat: this is puzzling: how is this different from two olive-bulks of fat? Nevertheless, now one cannot say that he separated the fat from the kidney and placed the kidney on the altar so that notar would take effect on it, since it does not speak of two limbs, that is, two pieces.
tosafot:a14.1: The throat does not hold more than two olive-bulks: that is, in the normal manner of eating.
tosafot:a15.1: Joining and carrying for Shabbat: that is, carrying was joined with the other labors for Shabbat, and carrying was not joined with the other labors for Yom Kippur. These are my teacher’s words, of blessed memory.
tosafot:a16.1: If it was Shabbat and he carried it out: And if you ask: what does this have to do with eating? One may say that this is its meaning: he carried it out in his mouth. Since he placed it in his mouth in the private domain and carried it out into the public domain, he is liable for carrying, since his swallowing is its placing down; for one who carries out and writes two letters while walking is liable, since their writing is their placing down.
tosafot:a19.1: Rather, Rafram’s is an error: In the chapter Shnei Se’irim (Yoma 66b) this passage also appears, and it does not reject it with “perhaps the scapegoat is different” as it rejects it here. Rather, it is common that words of Torah are poor in their place and rich in another place.
gershom:a1.1: [A printer’s marker at the start reads: “Up to here belongs to 13b.”] Granted that a prohibition taking effect on a prohibition, a mere one, he does not hold: for example, where one said, “An oath that I will not eat forbidden fat,” and ate it, he is liable only on account of the fat and not on account of the oath, and a prohibition does not take effect on a prohibition. And similarly a nazirite who said, “An oath that I will not eat grapes,” and ate. But where there is an expanded prohibition, where others were added to his prohibition, or an inclusive prohibition, where it includes permitted things together with forbidden things, for example a nazirite who said, “[An oath] that I will not eat figs and grapes,” and ate figs and grapes: since the prohibition of the oath took effect on the figs, it takes effect on the grapes as well. So too, wherever there is an expanded or an inclusive prohibition, he holds that a prohibition takes effect on a prohibition. And here too, a pure person was initially forbidden only in fat, but sacrificial food of lesser sanctity, or, if he was a priest, sacrificial food of the most sacred order, he could eat.
gershom:a2.1: He became impure; since he became forbidden in pure pieces: sacrificial food that was permitted to him before. This is inclusive, [since he became forbidden] in things permitted before; it was added also on the fat, that is, the prohibition of impurity [on] the prohibition of fat.
gershom:a3.1: He consecrated the fat; since the prohibition of benefit was added to it: for consecrated fat is forbidden for benefit to everyone. This is an expanded prohibition, since it adds others’ prohibition onto his prohibition; a prohibition was added also with regard to the fat. Therefore the prohibition of consecrated items also takes effect on the prohibition of fat and of impurity.
gershom:a4.1: And still, it is forbidden to an ordinary person: in eating and in benefit; but for the Most High it is permitted, for burning.
gershom:a5.1: It became notar: it is an expanded prohibition, since another [prohibition] was added onto its prohibition; the prohibition of notar was added onto it, onto the prohibition of fat.
gershom:a6.1: Yom Kippur took effect on it; since he became forbidden with regard to non-sacred food: this is an inclusive prohibition; the prohibition of Yom Kippur was added also onto the prohibition of fat.
gershom:a7.1: And let it also teach: liable to five sin offerings, and establish it: liable to a fifth sin offering, for example where he ate an olive-bulk of piggul from another animal.
gershom:a8.1: The mishna speaks of one animal, and notar and piggul are not found in one animal: since piggul arises only in the four rites, and once he had intent concerning it at the time of the rite to render it piggul, all of it became piggul at once and is not fit for eating, and it does not come to be notar.
gershom:a10.1: You find it in one animal, for example where he brought a piggul limb up to the altar: since he brought it up and the fire took hold of it, its piggul status was abrogated, and if he removed it and left it over, it is notar. And when he ate this limb whose piggul status was abrogated and which became notar, and ate an olive-bulk of piggul from the other piggul limbs of that same animal, let him be liable also for piggul, and both would be in one animal.
gershom:a11.1: And from where do we know that piggul status is abrogated in this way? As Ulla said in tractate Zevaḥim: a handful that is piggul that one brought up to the altar, once the fire has taken hold of it, [if] he took it down and left it over, its piggul status is abrogated and it becomes notar. Even so, the mishna speaks of one limb, for which he is liable, and notar and piggul are not found in one animal and in one limb.
gershom:a12.1: Why are they not found in one limb? For example, where he brought a piggul limb up to the altar and placed half the limb on the altar while half the limb hung outside the altar; then in one limb there would be notar and piggul. [The answer:] It is impossible for there to be [both] in one limb, since one cannot be so exact as to place precisely half of the limb; where the majority of the limb is, there we cast it, since you go after the majority.
gershom:a13.1: Resolve the dilemma that Rami bar Ḥama raised in [the chapter] Behema HaMaksha: does one follow the majority with regard to limbs or not? Rather, since it was not resolved for him from here, learn from this that we do not follow the majority of a limb; so let it be established in one limb as we said, and let him be liable also for piggul.
gershom:a14.1: Rather, the tanna of the mishna speaks of one olive-bulk, and in one olive-bulk you do not find piggul and notar: for if he placed half the olive-bulk on the altar and half outside, there is no burning of less than an olive-bulk, so its piggul status is not abrogated and it remains piggul. So you find piggul and notar in one limb only in a limb that has two olive-bulks of fat, and the tanna does not speak of two olive-bulks.
gershom:a15.1: And does it not? But it teaches Yom Kippur, and so on. Rabbi Zeira said: this is how you find it, that with regard to Yom Kippur it is a full measure and yet you do not find piggul and notar in it: for example, where he ate a kidney with its fat, the kidney being an olive-bulk and its fat an olive-bulk, and this is one limb. And in its fat, which is an olive-bulk, you cannot establish piggul and notar, as we said above, since there is no heikesh [so the printed text; above he said “no burning”] of less than an olive-bulk. And if you should wish to say, let him be liable for the kidney on account of piggul and for its fat on account of notar, you cannot say so, since it teaches “an impure person who ate fat” that is notar from consecrated items; evidently it wants to establish all the prohibitions in the fat itself, and piggul and notar are not found in one olive-bulk. And the olive-bulk of kidney comes only to complete the date-bulk, and one cannot say it is piggul, as we said.
gershom:a16.1: Rav Pappa said: With what are we dealing here, where he is liable to four sin offerings only? For example, where there was only an olive-bulk of fat, and he ate dates with it until he filled it out to a date-bulk, and one cannot establish piggul in it.
gershom:a17.1: Rav Aḥa bar Ya’akov, and so on [so Rabbeinu Gershom’s text; the daf reads Rav Adda bar Aḥa]. And he resolves it as where he ate, together with this olive-bulk of fat, an olive-bulk of piggul from another animal; and he does not answer with these answers that we answer, that it speaks of one animal, one limb and one olive-bulk. Rather, he holds that it speaks even of two animals and two olive-bulks.
gershom:a18.1: If so, let it teach: liable to six sin offerings, and establish it also where he ate a third olive-bulk, of blood.
gershom:a19.1: It speaks of one eating, that he can swallow together, and the Sages calculated, and so on. Therefore it does not teach blood.
gershom:a20.1: And let it also teach: if he carried it out on Yom Kippur he is liable. What is the reason it teaches: if it was Shabbat and he carried it out?
gershom:a21.1: Rafram said: That is to say, joining and carrying for Shabbat: that is, for Shabbat there is a prohibition to carry in courtyards without a joining [eruv], and there is a prohibition of carrying out from the private domain to the public domain; and there is no joining and carrying for Yom Kippur. [This follows] from the fact that it does not teach: and if he carried it out on Yom Kippur.
gershom:a22.1: Appointed: one who is accustomed to lead it into the wilderness. And even in impurity: even if the one leading it is impure. From the fact that it teaches “and even on Shabbat,” it was necessary to permit it on Shabbat and not on Yom Kippur: that is to say, joining, and so on.
gershom:a23.1: From where [is this proven]? I can tell you that there is joining and carrying for Yom Kippur too, for all other matters, and the scapegoat is different, [and for that reason] there is no prohibition of joining for it, since the fulfillment of its mitzva on Yom Kippur is in this, to lead it to the wilderness. Rather, Rafram’s is an error.
gershom:a24.1: There is one who engages in one act of intercourse, and so on; one who has intercourse with his daughter is liable for her on account of his daughter and his sister. That is, for example, where he had intercourse with his mother and fathered a daughter from her; and his brother from his father married her, and the brother who married her died; and his father’s brother, his uncle, married her and died; and afterward she married another man, and she is menstruating, and her father had intercourse with her. He is liable to six sin offerings: on account of his daughter, his sister, the wife of his brother, and so on.
rashi:b1.1: But Rabbi Meir does not hold, and so on: for above we wanted to establish it only with an inclusive and an expanded prohibition.
rashi:b2.1: Since a prohibition was added to her with regard to the other brothers: on account of a brother’s wife, a prohibition was added with regard to him too.
rashi:b3.1: She married his father’s brother; since a prohibition was added with regard to his brothers, it was added with regard to him: and with regard to his brothers, [she is forbidden] on account of the wife of the father’s brother. [Rashi’s lemma reads “his brothers”; the Davidson English reads “the sons of his father’s other brothers,” and the Aramaic of the daf “his father’s other brothers.”]
rashi:b3.2: Another version: we read, “since a prohibition was added with regard to the sons of his father’s brothers,” on account of a father’s wife.
rashi:b4.1: Mishna. His daughter’s daughter and his daughter-in-law: where his son married her.
rashi:b4.2: And his wife’s sister: where he was married to the daughter of his son-in-law, who is the sister of his daughter’s daughter through the father. For example, where he [the son-in-law] had a daughter from another wife, and this man, the father-in-law of his daughter’s husband, married her; and when this man had intercourse with the daughter of his son-in-law who is his daughter’s daughter, she was his wife’s sister.
rashi:b4.3: And the wife of his brother: where his son died and this man’s brother married her.
rashi:b4.4: And the wife of his father’s brother: where his brother died and his father’s brother married her.
rashi:b4.5: If the elder transgressed: this man’s father married her, and afterward this man had intercourse with her; he is liable also on account of a father’s wife.
rashi:b5.1: And likewise his wife’s daughter: he is liable for her on account of his wife’s daughter, his daughter-in-law, his brother’s wife, and so on. And likewise his wife’s daughter: he is liable for her on account of all of these.
rashi:b6.1: Gemara. Is she permitted to him: to this man’s father? But she is his brother’s wife, for we hold his son liable on account of the wife of his father’s brother; evidently she is forbidden to his father as a brother’s wife, and he has no marriage with her. So why does Rabbi Yosei say he is liable for her on account of a father’s wife?
rashi:b6.2: Where she happened to come before him for levirate marriage: from his brother who died without sons, and he came to take her in levirate marriage.
rashi:b7.1: If so, what is “transgressed”: the elder acted properly, since she is not forbidden to him by a prohibition of forbidden relations. And if you say: she is his daughter-in-law, for we hold his son liable on account of a brother’s wife, that is no refutation, for one can establish that she was the wife of his son’s brother from his mother, so that she is not the father’s daughter-in-law but the wife of his stepson, and she is permitted to him.
rashi:b7.2: That he transgressed on account of his son’s daughter-in-law, who is a secondary relative: by rabbinic law, for we held his son liable on account of [her being] his daughter-in-law. The same is true that he could have answered that he transgressed on account of his son’s daughter’s daughter, who is a secondary relative, but he took one of them.
rashi:b9.1: Two death penalties: his mother-in-law and a married woman, where there is burning and strangulation, and burning is more severe than strangulation.
rashi:b9.2: By the first prohibition: and not by the last, since a prohibition does not take effect on a prohibition.
rashi:b12.1: Rabbi Yosei concedes: in our mishna, where there is an expanded prohibition; the same applies to an inclusive prohibition and to a simultaneous one, as is explained below. Therefore, in the case of his mother-in-law who became a married woman, even though there is an expanded prohibition, since the prohibition of a married woman was added for everyone, even so he is judged on account of his mother-in-law, since it is more severe. But in the case of a married woman who became his mother-in-law, there is neither inclusive nor expanded.
rashi:b13.1: And here, in the case of his daughter’s daughter where his father transgressed and married her, what expanded prohibition is there, so that the prohibition of a father’s wife should be added for this one?
rashi:b13.2: Where the grandfather has a son: who is this man’s brother. Since a prohibition was added for that son on account of a father’s wife, it was added for this one too.
rashi:b15.1: Mishna. Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri says, and so on: on account of his mother-in-law and his mother-in-law’s mother, where he was married to her daughter and to her daughter’s daughter; and his father-in-law’s mother, where he married her son’s daughter.
rashi:b15.2: The three of them are one category: they are written in one verse and in one prohibition; therefore there is no division of sin offerings between them.
tosafot:b2.1: She married his brother; since a prohibition was added, and so on: that is, on account of a brother’s wife. And if you ask: but she is a mamzeret; if so, how is she forbidden to his brother on account of a brother’s wife? How does the prohibition of a brother’s wife take effect on the prohibition of a mamzeret? One may say that it speaks where his brother too is a mamzer, and so there is no prohibition of a mamzeret, since he himself is likewise a mamzer. And one may further say that a severe prohibition does take effect on a lighter prohibition, as I explained above.
tosafot:b3.1: Since a prohibition was added with regard to the sons of the brothers, and so on: these are two categories, a father’s wife and the wife of his father’s brother, in an expanded prohibition.
tosafot:b4.1: In brief: Rabbeinu Barukh asked why the mishna does not also count “her son’s daughter,” for example where his daughter married his wife’s son and bore him a daughter, who is at once his daughter’s daughter and his wife’s son’s daughter. And in the latter clause, why does it not teach “her son’s daughter and her daughter’s daughter”? This can be found where Jacob married Rachel and Leah, who are not sisters; Rachel had a son from another man, who married Leah’s daughter by Jacob; Leah’s daughter bore a daughter, and Jacob had intercourse with her, so that she is his wife’s son’s daughter and his daughter’s daughter. [Tosafot answer:] according to what is explained below, that the mishna speaks only of an expanded prohibition, this is well. The holy Rabbi Yom Tov asked why it does not teach “his mother-in-law,” for example where he married his daughter’s daughter’s daughter, so that his daughter’s daughter is his mother-in-law. One may say that the first tanna does not speak of one who committed a transgression [in marrying], and for this reason it does not teach his mother-in-law’s mother and his father-in-law’s mother, which are secondary relatives. Even according to Rabbi Yosei, who speaks of the elder who transgressed and married her, one may say it does not teach them because that would be an inclusive prohibition; and even according to Rabbi Ḥiyya, who says (Yevamot 32b–33a) that according to Rabbi Yosei one is liable to two on account of an inclusive prohibition, that is an inclusive prohibition within one category, but not in two categories. For this reason, according to him, it is well with regard to a married woman who became his mother-in-law, that we do not say he is judged on account of his mother-in-law, since they are two categories. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:b4.2: In brief: And his wife’s sister: the Ri says that this is not part of the text, for if so there would be seven, and instead of teaching six above it should teach seven. If you ask: let it teach seven [here] and count his wife’s sister, as where Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, married some man and bore him a daughter, that man had another daughter from another wife, and Jacob married her, so that Dinah’s daughter is Jacob’s daughter’s daughter and his wife’s sister, with the prohibition of a wife’s sister taking effect as an inclusive prohibition: one may say that the mishna teaches only prohibitions that Rabbi Yosei concedes, and the latter clause speaks of an expanded prohibition; and even according to Rabbi Ḥiyya, who says Rabbi Yosei holds by an inclusive prohibition, the mishna came to teach only an expanded prohibition. If you ask: why does it not teach his wife’s sister simultaneously, as where Jacob married [the man’s daughter, who would be] a half-sister of Dinah’s daughter, and [Dinah] then bore that daughter, so that she is at once his daughter’s daughter and his wife’s sister: one may say that, of prohibitions that come through betrothal, it counts only one that takes effect at the moment of betrothal, while here no prohibition existed when Jacob married until Dinah gave birth. If you ask: from where does the Gemara know that he concedes with regard to an expanded prohibition? Perhaps the whole mishna speaks of simultaneous prohibitions, as where she was betrothed under the age of three, so that at the end of her third year all the prohibitions take effect at once: one may say that it does not count a prohibition that comes through betrothal unless it takes effect at the time of betrothal, and here none took effect until the end of three years and one day; and further, that the mishna comes to teach only an expanded prohibition, as explained. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:b7.1: That he transgressed on account of his son’s daughter-in-law, a secondary relative: and the first tanna, since it is a rabbinic prohibition, does not count it.
tosafot:b12.1: Rabbi Yosei concedes with regard to an expanded prohibition: where a severe prohibition takes effect on a lighter prohibition, or with equal prohibitions, such as the prohibition of a brother[’s wife] and the prohibition of a wife’s sister; but a light one does not take effect on a severe one, even as an expanded prohibition. Therefore, his mother-in-law who became a married woman, and so on. And Rabbi Yosei, who comes to add the father’s wife, does not concede those that the first tanna mentioned. Granted, his daughter-in-law, [punished] by stoning, takes effect on his daughter’s daughter, [punished] by burning; and the father’s wife takes effect on his daughter-in-law, since the two are equal. But a married woman, [punished] by strangulation, does not take effect on burning and stoning; and all the more so a wife’s sister, a brother’s wife, the wife of his father’s brother and a menstruating woman, which carry mere karet, do not take effect. Therefore, according to Rabbi Yosei you find only three: his daughter’s daughter, his daughter-in-law and his father’s wife.
tosafot:b12.2: Rabbi Yosei concedes with regard to an expanded prohibition: Rashi explained that the same applies to an inclusive prohibition, but this does not seem so from the chapter Arba’a Aḥin [in Yevamot].
tosafot:b14.1: The wife of his brother: that is, the wife of his brother from his mother; for if from his father, how did the elder marry her? Betrothal would not take hold of her, since she is his daughter-in-law. From here it is implied that the wife of one’s maternal brother carries karet and one is liable to a sin offering for her; and what is excluded in Torat Kohanim is [only] from [the punishment of] childlessness, but there is karet.
gershom:b1.1: [A printer’s marker at the start reads: “Up to here belongs to 14a.”] One who has intercourse with his daughter’s daughter is liable for her on account of his daughter’s daughter and his daughter-in-law: for example, where his son married her, since one is permitted to marry one’s sister’s daughter, and she is his daughter-in-law.
gershom:b2.1: And his wife’s sister: for example, where the husband had a daughter from another wife, and his father-in-law married her [and fathered a daughter from her], and when this man had intercourse with his daughter’s daughter, she was his wife’s sister. And if his brother married her before that and died, and afterward his father’s brother married her and died, and afterward she was a married woman and menstruating, and afterward this man had intercourse with her, he is liable for her on account of his daughter’s daughter, his daughter-in-law, and so on.
gershom:b3.1: Rabbi Yosei says: If the elder transgressed and married her, his son’s daughter’s daughter, and afterward his son had intercourse with her, he is liable for her on account of a father’s wife. Even though his father had no marriage with her but married her in transgression, since she is not forbidden to him by Torah law, being a secondary relative, he is liable for her on account of a father’s wife.
gershom:b4.1: And likewise one who has intercourse with his wife’s daughter is liable for her in all these categories: on account of his wife’s daughter, his daughter-in-law, his wife’s sister, and so on; [his wife’s sister] for example where his wife’s daughter had a sister from another mother, and her mother’s husband married her; and his brother’s wife, for example where his brother married her after his son’s death, and afterward his father’s brother, and so on. And likewise one who has intercourse with his wife’s daughter’s daughter is liable for her on account of his wife’s daughter’s daughter and all these categories. And the same applies to one who has intercourse with her son’s daughter, in whom all these categories are found; but it teaches the daughter’s daughter, and the same applies to the son’s daughter.
gershom:b5.1: A simultaneous prohibition: for when he has intercourse with his daughter, the prohibitions of his daughter and his sister come together. She married his brother; since a prohibition was added with regard to all the brothers, where she is not bound to them for levirate marriage, it was added also with regard to him [on account of a brother]. This is an expanded prohibition, where others were added to his prohibition, since her prohibition applies also to all the brothers. She married his father’s brother: this too is an expanded prohibition, since she became forbidden also to his father’s brothers. And a married woman and a menstruating woman: this too is an expanded prohibition, since others too were added to his prohibition.
gershom:b6.1: Is she permitted to him: does the elder have betrothal with her, so that his son should be liable for her on account of a father’s wife?
gershom:b7.1: Yes; Rabbi Yoḥanan said: for example, where she happened to come before him for levirate marriage, since his son’s daughter’s daughter was married to the elder’s brother and came before him for levirate marriage.
gershom:b8.1: If so, if she came before him for levirate marriage, since by Torah law she is bound to him, as she is not one of the forbidden relations themselves, what is meant by “transgressed”?
gershom:b9.1: Yes, that he transgressed the words of the Sages, since he married a secondary relative: for his son’s daughter-in-law is a secondary relative, and so too his son’s daughter’s daughter; but it teaches his son’s daughter-in-law, and the same applies to his son’s daughter’s daughter.
gershom:b10.1: And so you find until the end of all generations: for his son’s son’s daughter and his son’s daughter’s daughter, until the end of all generations, are all secondary relatives.
gershom:b11.1: Does Rabbi Yosei hold that a prohibition takes effect on a prohibition, since it teaches: if the elder transgressed and married her, he is liable for her on account of a father’s wife? But we learned: one who committed a transgression, and so on.
gershom:b12.1: Rabbi Abbahu said: Rabbi Yosei concedes with regard to an expanded prohibition, where others were added to his prohibition, for there a prohibition takes effect on a prohibition. And if you say: his mother-in-law who became a married woman; here a prohibition was added with regard to another, with regard to everyone, so let him be liable to two in this way? Yes, certainly he is liable to two, but he cannot be executed with two executions; therefore he is judged by the first prohibition. And this is what it says there in Yevamot: the verse ascribes to him as though he did two, and he did one. What difference does it make? To bury him among the completely wicked, among those stoned and burned. But here, with regard to sin offerings, where there is an expanded prohibition, Rabbi Yosei concedes that he is liable to two, since a prohibition takes effect on a prohibition.
gershom:b13.1: And here, what expanded prohibition is there with regard to him, where the elder transgressed and married her?
gershom:b14.1: There is, for example where the grandfather has another son: since a prohibition was added with regard to his son, who is forbidden his father’s wife, a prohibition was added also with regard to this one.
gershom:b15.1: One who has intercourse with his daughter’s daughter, and so on, on account of his mother-in-law and his daughter-in-law [so the lemma reads; the explanation concerns the mother-in-law]: for example, where his mother-in-law was married to his son. And his wife’s sister: for example, where he was previously married to his mother-in-law’s sister. And his brother’s wife: for example, where his son died and his brother married her, and afterward his father’s brother married her and died, and afterward another man married her, and she is menstruating. And likewise one who has intercourse with his mother-in-law’s mother is liable for her on account of his mother-in-law’s mother, his daughter-in-law, his wife’s sister and all these categories.
gershom:b16.1: And likewise one who has intercourse with his father-in-law’s mother is liable for her on account of his father-in-law’s mother, his daughter-in-law, his wife’s sister, and so on.
gershom:b17.1: Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri said: One who has intercourse with his mother-in-law is liable for her on account of his mother-in-law, his mother-in-law’s mother and his father-in-law’s mother. How so? For example, where his mother-in-law had two daughters and one son, and he married one daughter, and married her brother’s daughter and her sister’s daughter; when he has intercourse with the elderly mother-in-law, she is his mother-in-law, his mother-in-law’s mother and his father-in-law’s mother. They said to him: The three of them are one category, the category of mother-in-law, and he is liable to only one sin offering.
